title: India Plans Gold Monetisation Revamp to Unlock $5 Trillion in Household Reserves
excerpt: The government is expected to announce a restructured scheme within weeks, bringing jewellers into the collection network to mobilise more than 1,000 tonnes of idle gold.
body:
• Indian households, temples and institutions hold an estimated 25,000–30,000 tonnes of gold worth nearly $5.2 trillion — more than the combined reserves of the world's 10 largest central banks.
  • The government is expected to announce a revamped Gold Monetisation Scheme within weeks, allowing jewellers across the country to collect household gold deposits for the first time.
  • India's gold import bill hit a record $71.98 billion in FY2025-26, up 24% year-on-year, making gold the second-largest import after crude oil.
  • Since its 2015 launch, the existing scheme has mobilised only about 39 tonnes of gold — a fraction of a percent of total household holdings.

India's central government is preparing to overhaul its Gold Monetisation Scheme in a fresh attempt to channel the country's massive private gold reserves into the formal financial system, according to multiple reports citing government sources.

The revamped framework, expected to be announced within weeks after consultations with the Reserve Bank of India, commercial banks and bullion industry representatives, would for the first time allow jewellers to act as collection partners — a significant departure from the current bank-only model.

The Scale of India's Dormant Gold Wealth

Indian households are estimated to hold between 25,000 and 30,000 tonnes of physical gold in home safes, lockers and vaults, according to a June 2026 NSE Market Pulse report. At current market prices, these holdings are valued at approximately ₹375 lakh crore, or $4.46 trillion. Including the 3,000–4,000 tonnes held by temples and institutional trusts, India's total private gold stock reaches an estimated $5.2 trillion — roughly 125% of the country's nominal GDP.

That wealth, however, remains almost entirely outside the productive economy. Unlike equities, bonds or bank deposits, idle gold generates no returns and contributes nothing to capital formation.

Why Previous Efforts Failed

The Gold Monetisation Scheme, launched in 2015 under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, was designed to reduce India's dependence on gold imports by encouraging households and institutions to deposit idle gold with banks in exchange for interest income. Banks could then refine and recycle the metal for jewellery manufacturers, reducing the need for fresh imports.

The results have been underwhelming. By March 2025, only about 38 tonnes of gold had entered the scheme — barely 0.15% of India's estimated household holdings. Industry executives told Moneycontrol the total has since inched up to roughly 39 tonnes.

"An effective and sound GMS has long been a missing lever in India's gold sector reform agenda. The strength of any revamped GMS will ultimately rest on the integrity of the refining backbone."

— Samit Guha, MD & CEO, MMTC-PAMP

Several factors limited participation: emotional attachment to family jewellery, reluctance to melt heirloom ornaments, low interest rates — currently 0.5% to 0.6% annually — limited awareness and the logistical burden of visiting bank branches for purity testing.

What the Revamp Would Change

Under the proposed framework, jewellers nationwide would be authorised to collect gold from households, conduct initial purity checks and route deposits to authorised refiners and banks. In return, jewellers would receive a service fee for mobilising deposits and processing transactions.

The All India Gems and Jewellery Domestic Council (AIGJDC) has proposed allowing dematerialised gold balances — digital units backed by physical gold held in regulated bank accounts — to replace the current certificate-based system. Industry experts argue this would improve compliance, reduce handling costs and make gold function as an interest-bearing financial asset rather than a passive store of value.

The government discontinued medium-term (5–7 years, 2.25% interest) and long-term (12–15 years, 2.5%) deposit options in March 2025. Only the short-term bank deposit, with a tenure of one to three years, remains available.

The Import Bill Pressure

The urgency behind the revamp is driven in part by India's ballooning gold import bill. The country imported a record $71.98 billion worth of gold in FY2025-26, a 24% increase from the previous year, according to the NSE report. Gold accounted for more than 9% of India's total merchandise imports, second only to crude oil, and contributed to a widening trade deficit of $333.2 billion.

The proposed revamp follows PM Modi's appeal to citizens earlier this year to avoid buying gold for one year, made during heightened uncertainty from the West Asia conflict. The RBI's latest Financial Stability Report noted that gold import growth "decelerated substantially" in May, with imports falling to around $12 billion — the third straight monthly decline.

What's Next

If even a small fraction of India's private gold enters the formal system, the macroeconomic implications could be significant. Mobilising just 5% — roughly 1,250 tonnes — would exceed India's annual gold demand and could meaningfully reduce import dependence while freeing capital for productive investment.

The government is expected to finalise the revamped scheme after completing industry consultations, with an announcement likely timed ahead of the festive season, when gold demand traditionally surges.
nri_angle: NRI investors with family gold holdings in India could benefit from the revamped scheme's digital gold balances and improved accessibility.
author: Diaspora Desk
